problem.text: In some countries, automobile fuel efficiency is measured in liters per $100$ kilometers while other countries use miles per gallon. Suppose that $1$ kilometer equals $m$ miles, and $1$ gallon equals $\ell$ liters. Which of the following gives the fuel efficiency in liters per $100$ kilometers for a car that gets $x$ miles per gallon?

steps.title: Where to start: follow one trip
steps.body: "Liters per $100$ kilometers" asks a concrete question: how many liters does the car burn on a $100$ km trip? So follow that trip through the units: kilometers to miles, miles to gallons, gallons to liters.

your_turn.answer: $100m$ miles, since each kilometer is $m$ miles.

steps.title: Miles to gallons
steps.body: The car goes $x$ miles on each gallon. So a trip of $d$ miles uses $\frac{d}{x}$ gallons. For example, $60$ miles at $30$ miles per gallon uses $2$ gallons.

your_turn.prompt: How many gallons does the $100m$-mile trip use?
your_turn.answer: $\frac{100m}{x}$ gallons: divide the miles by the miles per gallon.

steps.title: Know which way each letter should push
steps.body: Before the last conversion, decide what a correct answer must do. A car with higher mpg $x$ is more efficient, so it burns fewer liters. A bigger $\ell$ means each gallon holds more liters, and a bigger $m$ means $100$ km is a longer drive in miles, so both should give more liters.

your_turn.prompt: Which answer choices have $x$ in the denominator and $\ell$ and $m$ in the numerator?
your_turn.answer: (C) and (E). The other three each fail at least one check, so the last conversion only has to decide between these two.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Each gallon is $\ell$ liters, so the trip uses $$\frac{100m}{x}\cdot \ell = \frac{100\ell m}{x} \text{ liters}.$$ It goes down when $x$ grows and up when $\ell$ or $m$ grows, just as it should. The answer is **(E)** $\frac{100\ell m}{x}$.

wrong_choices.A: This is the rate turned upside down: it measures distance per fuel, not fuel per distance. You can spot it because it gets bigger when $x$ gets bigger, but a more efficient car should use fewer liters.
wrong_choices.D: This comes from applying both conversions backwards, dividing by $m$ to turn kilometers into miles and dividing by $\ell$ to turn gallons into liters. Check: a bigger $\ell$ should mean more liters, but here it gives fewer.

verification.verifier_notes: Passed adversarial verifier on first review.
